message.content:
### Your Rights as a Tenant in Texas (as of 2026) Below is a concise overview of the key protections and responsibilities that apply to residential tenants in Texas. These rights are derived from state statutes (primarily the Texas Property Code), local ordinances, and general landlord‑tenant law. For specific situations—especially those involving disputes, evictions, or lease negotiations—consult a qualified attorney or your local tenant‑rights organization. | Area | What You’re Entitled To | How to Exercise It | |------|------------------------|--------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to **one month’s rent** for a furnished unit and **two months’ rent** for an unfurnished unit.
• Deposit must be returned within **30 days** after you move out, minus any lawful deductions. | • Keep a written record of the unit’s condition (photos, video, or a move‑in/move‑out inspection checklist).
• Request a written itemized statement of deductions if the landlord withholds part of the deposit. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a **safe, sanitary, and livable condition** (e.g., functioning plumbing, heating, electrical, pest control). | • Report problems in writing (email or certified mail) and give the landlord a reasonable time to fix them. | | **Repair & Maintenance** | • If the landlord fails to repair, you may:
 1. **Withhold rent** (only after giving written notice and a 10‑day cure period).
 2. **Make the repair yourself** and deduct the cost from rent (must be reasonable and documented).
 3. **File a complaint** with the Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA) or local code enforcement. | • Keep receipts and a written record of all communications. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlord must give **reasonable notice** (usually 24 hours) before entering, except in emergencies. | • Document any unannounced entries; you can file a complaint if the landlord repeatedly violates this rule. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected under the **Fair Housing Act** and Texas law: no discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income. | • File a complaint with the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) or the Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR). | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease agreements must be in writing for **any term longer than one year**. | • Review the lease carefully; any ambiguous or illegal clauses can be challenged. | | **Rent Increases** | • No statutory limit on rent increases, but the landlord must provide **written notice** (usually 30 days for month‑to‑month leases). | • Verify that the increase is not retaliatory or discriminatory. | | **Eviction** | • Landlord must follow the **Texas Property Code** eviction process: written notice, filing a lawsuit, and obtaining a court order.
• Common grounds: non‑payment of rent, lease violations, or landlord’s intent to occupy the unit. | • Respond promptly to notices; consider negotiating a payment plan or settlement. | | **Right to Repair** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major issue, you may **pay for the repair** and deduct the cost from rent, provided you give notice and keep records. | • Use a reputable contractor and obtain a written estimate. | | **Security Deposit Deductions** | • Landlord may deduct for:
 • Unpaid rent
 • Damage beyond normal wear and tear
 • Cleaning costs if the unit is not left in a reasonable condition | • Dispute any deduction you believe is unjustified; you can file a claim in small claims court. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Generally allowed if the lease permits it or if the landlord consents. | • Obtain written permission; keep a copy of the sublease agreement. | | **Utilities** | • Landlord must provide essential utilities (water, heat, electricity) unless otherwise specified. | • Verify utility responsibilities in the lease. | | **Legal Remedies** | • **Small Claims Court**: recover unpaid rent or damages up to $20,000.
• **Civil Court**: for larger claims or eviction disputes. | • Keep all documentation (rent receipts, correspondence, photos). | --- #### Quick Checklist for Tenants 1. **Read Your Lease** – Understand all terms, especially regarding rent, deposits, maintenance, and entry. 2. **Document Everything** – Photos, videos, written notices, and receipts help protect you. 3. **Know the Notice Periods** – 24‑hour notice for entry, 30‑day notice for rent increases, 30‑day notice for termination of month‑to‑month tenancy. 4. **Report Problems Promptly** – Give the landlord written notice and a reasonable cure period. 5. **Keep Records of Repairs** – If you pay for repairs, keep receipts and a written estimate. 6. **Know When to Seek Legal Help** – Evictions, disputes over deposits, or significant habitability issues often require professional advice. --- #### Resources | Resource | What It Offers | How to Access | |----------|----------------|---------------| | **Texas Department of Housing and Community Affairs (TDHCA)** | Tenant‑landlord dispute resolution, housing assistance | https://www.tdhca.state.tx.us | | **Texas Commission on Human Rights (TCHR)** | Fair housing complaints | https://www.tchr.texas.gov | | **HUD (U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development)** | Federal fair housing enforcement | https://www.hud.gov | | **Local Tenant‑Rights Organizations** | Legal clinics, workshops, advocacy | Search online for “tenant rights Texas” + your city | | **Texas Small Claims Court** | Filing for damages up to $20,000 | https://www.txcourts.gov/small-claims/ | --- #### When to Call an Attorney - **Eviction Notice**: If you receive a notice to vacate, especially if you believe it’s retaliatory or unlawful. - **Disputed Security Deposit**: If the landlord refuses to return your deposit or disputes deductions. - **Major Habitability Issues**: Persistent problems that the landlord refuses to fix. - **Lease Disputes**: Ambiguous or potentially illegal lease clauses. --- **Bottom Line:** As a Texas tenant, you have the right to a safe, habitable home, privacy, fair treatment, and a clear, enforceable lease. By staying informed, documenting everything, and knowing when to seek help, you can protect your rights and address problems effectively.
